title: Armorum iudicium. Aiax
titleEn: Ajax Claims the Arms — Metamorphoses XIII.1–139
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The Greek chiefs take their seats, and Ajax, master of the sevenfold shield, rises first to claim the armour of Achilles: he sets his own fighting, done in front of witnesses, against deeds he says Ulysses does by night, presses his descent from Jupiter through Aeacus and Telamon, and charges his rival with feigned madness, with the abandoning of the son of Poeas and of Nestor, and with contriving the charge that destroyed Palamedes. He ends by proposing that the arms be flung among the Trojans and given to whoever fetches them back; the part closes with Ulysses on his feet and the opening of his reply.

sentences.t:
Consedere duces, et vulgi stante corona
surgit ad hos clipei dominus septemplicis Aiax,
sentences.l: The chiefs sat down, and with the ring of the crowd standing round, Ajax, master of the sevenfold shield, rises to face them,
sentences.i: The chiefs took their seats, and with the crowd standing round them in a ring, Ajax, lord of the seven-layered shield, rose to face them,
sentences.n: Consedere is the poetic third-plural perfect in -ere for consederunt, a standard verse form; valuere at line 89 is the same. Consido is also the ordinary word for a council or a court taking its seat. Vulgi stante corona is an ablative absolute, literally “with the crowd's ring standing”, and corona is the standing circle of onlookers round a hearing. Note the tense shift: consedere is perfect, surgit present. Clipei ... septemplicis, “of the sevenfold shield”, is split around dominus.

sentences.t:
utque erat impatiens irae, Sigeia torvo
litora respexit classemque in litore vultu
intendensque manus “agimus, pro Iuppiter!” inquit
“ante rates causam, et mecum confertur Ulixes!
sentences.l: and as he was unable to hold in his anger, he looked back at the Sigean shores and the fleet on the shore with grim face, and stretching out his hands he says: “We are pleading our case before the ships, O Jupiter! — and Ulysses is set beside me!
sentences.i: and since he could not contain his anger he turned a grim look back on the Sigean shore and the fleet drawn up along it, and flinging out his hands he said: “Before the ships, O Jupiter, we are pleading a case — and Ulysses is matched against me!
sentences.n: Causam agere is the Roman courtroom phrase “to plead a case”, and it governs the whole speech; Ajax opens as a pleader and closes on the same verb at line 120. Pro here is the interjection “O!” taking the vocative Iuppiter, not the preposition pro “in return for, on behalf of” that appears at lines 94 and 138. Impatiens takes the genitive irae, “not able to hold in his anger”. Torvo ... vultu is an ablative of manner split so that torvo ends line 3 and vultu ends line 4. Confertur is passive: Ulysses “is being set beside” him.

sentences.t:
At non Hectoreis dubitavit cedere flammis,
quas ego sustinui, quas hac a classe fugavi.
sentences.l: But he did not hesitate to give way before Hector's flames, which I withstood, which I routed from this fleet.
sentences.i: Ulysses, though, had no hesitation about retreating before Hector's fires — the fires I stood up to, the fires I drove back from this fleet.
sentences.n: Hectoreis is an adjective made from the name, “Hectorean”, and cedere takes the dative: to yield to the fires Hector brought. Non dubitavit is sarcasm — Ajax means Ulysses was quick enough about it. Fugavi normally means “put to flight” a person or an army; used of flames it treats the fire as an enemy routed.

sentences.t:
Tutius est igitur fictis contendere verbis,
quam pugnare manu!
sentences.l: It is safer, then, to contend with made-up words than to fight with the hand!
sentences.i: Safer, then, to do one's fighting with invented words than with the hand!
sentences.n: Contendere covers both a contest at law and a fight in the field, and Ajax works the double sense; he throws the same verb back as a challenge to combat at line 79. Fictis verbis, “with fabricated words”, is his charge, not the poem's: fingo returns at line 59 of an invented accusation and at line 67 of the charges he is himself making. Manu, “with the hand”, is the standing Latin way of saying “in hand-to-hand fighting”.

sentences.t:
Sed nec mihi dicere promptum,
nec facere est isti:
sentences.l: But neither is speaking ready to hand for me, nor doing for that fellow there:
sentences.i: But I have no gift for speaking, and he has none for doing:
sentences.n: Promptum est with a dative, “is ready to hand for”, has to be understood a second time with facere. Iste, here the dative isti, is the contemptuous demonstrative — that man on the other side of the case; Ajax uses it of Ulysses again at lines 19, 37, 58 and 117, and mostly declines to use his name.

sentences.t:
quantumque ego Marte feroci
quantum acie valeo, tantum valet iste loquendo.
sentences.l: and as much as I am strong in fierce war, as much as in the battle line, so much is that man strong in talking.
sentences.i: As strong as I am in the fierce work of war, as strong as I am in the line, that is how strong he is at talking.
sentences.n: The correlation is quantum ... quantum ... tantum, “as much ... as much ... so much”, the repeated quantum being anaphora rather than a second idea. Marte is Mars for the war he presides over, and acies is the drawn-up battle line. Magnus prints quantum acie valeo; some editions print inque acie, “and in the battle line”, which turns the second limb into a simple addition instead of a repetition. Loquendo is an ablative gerund, “by talking”.

sentences.t:
Nec memoranda tamen vobis mea facta, Pelasgi,
esse reor: vidistis enim.
sentences.l: Yet I do not think that my deeds are to be recounted to you, Pelasgians: for you have seen them.
sentences.i: And yet I do not think my deeds need any recounting to you, Pelasgians: you saw them yourselves.
sentences.n: Memoranda ... esse is a gerundive in indirect statement after reor, “that they must be recounted”. The dative vobis with a gerundive is normally the agent, “by you”, but the sense wanted here is the person told, “to you”, which vidistis explains. Reor is deponent: passive in form, active in meaning. Pelasgi is one of several names for the Greeks in this speech, beside Achivi at line 29 and Danai at line 92.

sentences.t:
Sua narret Ulixes,
quae sine teste gerit, quorum nox conscia sola est.
sentences.l: Let Ulysses tell his own deeds, which he does without a witness, of which night alone is in the secret.
sentences.i: Let Ulysses tell his own — the deeds he does with no witness by, the ones night alone knows about.
sentences.n: Narret is a jussive subjunctive, “let him tell”. Testis is the courtroom word for a witness, and conscia is close to it, “sharing the knowledge”, taking the genitive quorum. Sua, “his own things”, has no noun and answers mea facta in the line before. The charge is that Ulysses' exploits are unwitnessed, Ajax's way of calling them unverifiable.

sentences.t:
Praemia magna peto, fateor; sed demit honorem
aemulus:
sentences.l: Great prizes I seek, I admit; but a rival takes away the honour:
sentences.i: Yes, I am after a great prize, I admit it; but having such a rival cheapens it:
sentences.n: Fateor, “I admit”, is deponent and is a pleader's move: concede a point, then turn it. Demit honorem aemulus means that being matched against this opponent lowers the worth of the prize, not that the rival carries it off. Magnus prints peto, “I seek”; some editions print peti, which makes the sentence “I admit that great prizes are being sought”.

sentences.t:
Aiaci non est tenuisse superbum,
sit licet hoc ingens, quidquid speravit Ulixes.
sentences.l: for Ajax it is no proud thing to have held whatever Ulysses has hoped for, however huge that may be.
sentences.i: There is no pride for Ajax in having won a thing Ulysses so much as hoped for, however great it is.
sentences.n: The subject of est is the perfect infinitive tenuisse, and superbum is its neuter predicate: “to have held is not a proud thing”. Sit licet is the concessive idiom with the subjunctive, “granted that it be”, with licet standing after its verb. Ajax speaks of himself in the third person by name, as he does again at line 97.

sentences.t:
Iste tulit pretium iam nunc temptaminis huius,
quod, cum victus erit, mecum certasse feretur.
sentences.l: That man has already now carried off the reward of this attempt, in that, when he has been beaten, he will be said to have contended with me.
sentences.i: He has taken his winnings from this bid already: when he loses, the report will still be that he went up against me.
sentences.n: Quod here is “in that, in the fact that”, spelling out what the pretium consists of. Feretur is the passive of fero in the sense “is reported, is spoken of”. Certasse is the syncopated perfect infinitive for certavisse, a normal verse contraction. Cum victus erit is future perfect: Ajax treats the defeat as already settled.

sentences.t:
Atque ego, si virtus in me dubitabilis esset,
nobilitate potens essem, Telamone creatus,
moenia qui forti Troiana sub Hercule cepit
litoraque intravit Pagasaea Colcha carina.
sentences.l: And I, if my valour were doubtful in me, would be strong in birth, born of Telamon, who took the Trojan walls under brave Hercules and entered the Colchian shores in the Pagasaean keel.
sentences.i: And even if my courage were in question, I would still have my birth to stand on: I am Telamon's son, and he took the walls of Troy serving under Hercules, and reached the shores of Colchis in the ship built at Pagasae.
sentences.n: A present contrary-to-fact condition, esset in the if-clause and essem in the main clause: “if it were ... I would be”. Creatus with the plain ablative Telamone is the participle of origin, “born from”; the same idiom returns as cretus at line 31 and satus at line 123. Sub Hercule is “under Hercules' command”. Pagasaea carina names the ship from the Thessalian port where it was built, and Colcha litora its landfall; moenia ... Troiana is pulled apart by qui forti.

sentences.t:
Aeacus huic pater est, qui iura silentibus illic
reddit, ubi Aeoliden saxum grave Sisyphon urget.
sentences.l: Aeacus is father to him, who renders judgements to the silent ones there, where the heavy stone presses Sisyphus son of Aeolus.
sentences.i: His father is Aeacus, who administers justice to the silent dead down where the heavy stone bears down on Sisyphus, Aeolus' son.
sentences.n: Iura reddere is the technical phrase for a magistrate dispensing justice; Ajax puts a judge at the head of his own family while judgement is being passed on him. Silentibus, “the silent ones”, is a standing name for the dead. Aeoliden and Sisyphon keep Greek accusative endings; saxum grave is the subject of urget and Sisyphon its object. Sisyphus is brought in for a purpose — Ajax makes him Ulysses' real father at line 32.

sentences.t:
Aeacon agnoscit summus prolemque fatetur
Iuppiter esse suam: sic a Iove tertius Aiax.
sentences.l: Highest Jupiter acknowledges Aeacus and admits that he is his own offspring: so Ajax is third from Jove.
sentences.i: Jupiter on high owns Aeacus and admits the son is his: so Ajax stands third in descent from Jove.
sentences.n: Prolem ... esse suam is an accusative and infinitive after fatetur, its subject Aeacon carried over from the first clause. Summus and Iuppiter belong together and are split across the line-end, with prolemque fatetur standing between them. Tertius a Iove counts the generations the speech has just named: Aeacus, then Telamon, then Ajax.

sentences.t:
Nec tamen haec series in causam prosit, Achivi,
si mihi cum magno non est communis Achille:
sentences.l: Yet let this line of descent not help toward my case, Achaeans, if it is not shared by me with great Achilles:
sentences.i: And yet let none of this ancestry count in my case, Achaeans, unless I share it with great Achilles:
sentences.n: Prosit is a jussive subjunctive, “let it not help”, the same use as ne prosit at line 135. In causam is forensic: causa is the case being tried, the word Ajax used at line 6. Series is a line or succession of ancestors. Communis takes the dative mihi and the phrase cum ... Achille, Achille being the ablative of the name.

sentences.t: frater erat, fraterna peto!
sentences.l: He was a brother, I claim a brother's things!
sentences.i: He was my brother; what I am claiming is a brother's.
sentences.n: Fraterna is a neuter plural adjective used as a noun, “a brother's things”, what belongs to a brother by right. Frater is used loosely of a cousin: line 41 calls the armour dona patruelia, the gifts of a father's brother's son, so the two are cousins on their fathers' side. Peto is the verb for laying claim at law, used already of the praemia at line 16.

sentences.t:
Quid sanguine cretus
Sisyphio furtisque et fraude simillimus illi
inseris Aeacidis alienae nomina gentis?
sentences.l: Why do you, sprung from Sisyphian blood and most like him in thefts and in fraud, thrust the names of an alien house in among the sons of Aeacus?
sentences.i: Why do you, who come of Sisyphus' blood and are his very image in thieving and trickery, force an outsider's name in among the line of Aeacus?
sentences.n: Cretus, like creatus at line 22, takes a plain ablative of origin, sanguine Sisyphio. That Ulysses is Sisyphus' son and not Laertes' is Ajax's charge, and he uses the patronymic Laertiades himself at line 48; the poem does not endorse either. Simillimus takes the dative illi, pointing back to Sisyphus. Furtis “thefts” and fraude “fraud” are the accusations the whole speech keeps returning to, and Ajax means them as crimes, not as praise of cunning.

sentences.t:
An quod in arma prior nulloque sub indice veni,
arma neganda mihi, potiorque videbitur ille,
sentences.l: Or is it because I came into arms first and under no informer that arms are to be denied me, and that man will seem the better,
sentences.i: Or is this it — that because I came to the war first, with no informer needed, the arms are to be refused me, and he will look the worthier man,
sentences.n: An introduces an indignant question, and the quod clause supplies the alleged reason, “because”. Index is the informer who denounces or exposes a man; nullo sub indice means Ajax needed nobody to expose him, since he came of his own accord. Arma neganda mihi is a gerundive with sunt left out, “arms are to be denied me”. Videbitur is “will seem”, not “will be seen”: the passive of video regularly carries that sense.

sentences.t:
ultima qui cepit detrectavitque furore
militiam ficto, donec sollertior isto
et sibi inutilior timidi commenta retexit
Naupliades animi vitataque traxit ad arma?
sentences.l: the man who took them up last, and shirked service by a feigned madness, until the son of Nauplius, shrewder than that fellow and less useful to himself, laid bare the contrivances of a fearful mind and dragged him to the arms he had shunned?
sentences.i: the man who came to arms last of all, and dodged the service by faking madness, until Nauplius' son — cleverer than him, and far less use to himself — exposed the coward's inventions and hauled him off to the war he had ducked?
sentences.n: Ultima is a neuter plural used adverbially with cepit, “took them up last”. Furore ... ficto is an ablative of means, furore closing line 36 and ficto standing second in line 37 with militiam in front of it. Sollertior and inutilior are comparatives with isto as ablative of comparison. Retexit is the perfect of retego “uncover, expose”, matched by the perfect traxit in the same clause. Timidi at line 38 and animi at line 39 belong together, “of a fearful mind”, with commenta retexit Naupliades standing between them. Magnus prints et sibi inutilior; some editions print sed, which sharpens the paradox into a contrast.

sentences.t:
Optima num sumat, quia sumere noluit ulla:
nos inhonorati et donis patruelibus orbi,
obtulimus quia nos ad prima pericula, simus?
sentences.l: Is he to take the best arms, because he refused to take any: and are we to be unhonoured and stripped of our cousin's gifts, because we offered ourselves to the first dangers?
sentences.i: Is he to have the best arms because he would not take any? And are we to go unhonoured and robbed of a cousin's legacy because we put ourselves in the way of the first danger?
sentences.n: Num sumat and simus are indignant deliberative subjunctives, questions built to be answered no. Orbi takes the ablative donis, “bereft of the gifts”. Patruelibus means “belonging to a father's brother's son”, that is a cousin's, which fixes the sense of frater at line 31. Quia is postponed to second place in its clause after obtulimus, a displacement verse takes freely with conjunctions.

sentences.t:
Atque utinam aut verus furor ille, aut creditus esset,
nec comes hic Phrygias umquam venisset ad arces
hortator scelerum.
sentences.l: And would that that madness had either been real, or been believed, and that this man had never come as a companion to the Phrygian citadels, an urger of crimes!
sentences.i: How I wish that madness had been genuine, or at least believed — and that this man had never come along to the citadels of Phrygia, an instigator of crimes!
sentences.n: Utinam introduces a wish for what did not happen. The one verb esset serves both limbs: with the adjective verus, and with the participle creditus, where it makes a pluperfect passive, “had been believed”. Esset is imperfect, but the wish looks back to the past, as the pluperfect venisset in the next line shows. Hortator scelerum stands in apposition to hic, and it is Ajax's verdict delivered before his evidence. Phrygias arces means Troy.

sentences.t:
Non te, Poeantia proles,
expositum Lemnos nostro cum crimine haberet!
sentences.l: Lemnos would not be holding you, offspring of Poeas, cast out, with the reproach of it on us!
sentences.i: Lemnos would not have you there, son of Poeas, put ashore and left, and the shame of it ours!
sentences.n: Haberet is an imperfect subjunctive continuing the unreal wish, “would not be holding”. Ajax turns aside from the assembly to address an absent man — this turning-aside recurs at line 83, where he addresses Ulysses by name. The man addressed is Philoctetes, son of Poeas, whom lines 51 and 52 identify as the heir of Hercules' arrows. Expositum is the technical word for a person put ashore and abandoned. Crimen is again the charge or reproach, and this one Ajax admits lies against the Greeks.

sentences.t:
Qui nunc, ut memorant, silvestribus abditus antris
saxa moves gemitu Laertiadaeque precaris
quae meruit:
sentences.l: You who now, as men tell, hidden in woodland caves, move the rocks with your groaning and pray for the son of Laertes what he has deserved:
sentences.i: You who now, so they say, hidden away in caves in the woods, move the very rocks with your groaning and call down on Laertes' son exactly what he has earned:
sentences.n: Qui is a connecting relative opening a new sentence, “and you, who ...”, and moves is second person, so the apostrophe is still running. Ut memorant, “as they relate”, marks this as report: Ajax does not claim to have seen it. Precor takes a dative of the person prayed about, Laertiadae, and an accusative of the thing prayed for, quae meruit; here the thing is punishment. Laertiades, “son of Laertes”, is the very descent he refused to allow at line 32.

sentences.t: quae, si di sunt, non vana precaris!
sentences.l: things which, if there are gods, you do not pray in vain!
sentences.i: and if there are gods at all, you are not praying them in vain!
sentences.n: Quae picks up the quae of the line before, the things prayed for; vana is a neuter plural agreeing with it and doing adverbial work, “not in vain”. Si di sunt is a plain indicative condition, and Ajax leaves the doubt inside it standing.

sentences.t:
Et nunc ille eadem nobis iuratus in arma,
heu! pars una ducum, quo successore sagittae
Herculis utuntur, fractus morboque fameque
velaturque aliturque avibus, volucresque petendo
debita Troianis exercet spicula fatis.
sentences.l: And now that man, sworn with us into the same campaign — alas, one of our chieftains, whom Hercules' arrows make use of as their successor — broken by disease and by hunger, is both clothed and fed by birds, and by hunting birds he plies the shafts owed to the fates of Troy.
sentences.i: And now the man who took the oath into this same war along with us — one of our chiefs, God help him, the man Hercules' arrows now use as their heir — broken by sickness and starvation, gets his clothing and his food from birds, and shooting birds is how he keeps in practice the shafts Troy's fate is owed.
sentences.n: Iuratus is a perfect participle with active force, “having sworn”, and in arma is “into the campaign”. Quo successore ... utuntur is utor with its regular ablative: Hercules' arrows “make use of him as their successor”. Fractus takes the ablatives morbo and fame. Velaturque aliturque is the doubled -que ... -que of verse, “both ... and”, and both verbs are passive. Volucres petendo is a gerund governing an accusative object, a verse licence where prose would write volucribus petendis; the same construction returns at line 118. Debita ... fatis is split around Troianis exercet spicula.

sentences.t: Ille tamen vivit, quia non comitavit Ulixen;
sentences.l: Yet he is alive, because he did not accompany Ulysses;
sentences.i: He is alive, at any rate, because he did not go along with Ulysses;
sentences.n: Comitavit is the active form of a verb normally deponent, comitor; both are found, and the active suits the verse. Ulixen keeps the Greek accusative in -en, like Aeacon, Sisyphon, Nestora and Dolona elsewhere in the speech. The sting is in quia: Ajax makes the man's survival a result of having been abandoned.

sentences.t:
mallet et infelix Palamedes esse relictus:
viveret aut certe letum sine crimine haberet!
sentences.l: Unlucky Palamedes too would rather have been left behind: he would be alive, or at least would have a death with no charge on it!
sentences.i: Poor Palamedes would have preferred to be left behind himself: he would still be alive, or at least his death would carry no accusation!
sentences.n: Mallet, viveret and haberet are imperfect subjunctives of the unreal present, “would prefer”, “would be alive”. Esse relictus is a perfect passive infinitive after mallet, “to have been left”. Et is the adverb “also”, joining Palamedes to the man just addressed. Crimen is once more the formal charge, and sine crimine is a death with no accusation attached to it.

sentences.t:
Quem male convicti nimium memor iste furoris
prodere rem Danaam finxit fictumque probavit
crimen et ostendit, quod iam praefoderat, aurum.
sentences.l: And him that man, too mindful of the madness exposed to his cost, made out to be betraying the Danaan cause, and proved the fabricated charge, and produced the gold that he had buried there beforehand.
sentences.i: And him — with that exposed pretence of madness still rankling — Ulysses framed as a traitor to the Greek cause, made the invented charge stick, and dug up the gold he had planted himself.
sentences.n: Quem is a connecting relative, “and him”, object of finxit. Fingo with an accusative and infinitive is “to make out that”: prodere rem Danaam, “that he was betraying the Danaan state”. Fictum ... crimen answers finxit at once — the charge is invented and then proved. Memor takes the genitive furoris with male convicti agreeing; male can be “to his cost” or “wrongly”, and both have been read. Praefoderat, “had dug in beforehand”, makes the planting deliberate, and the relative clause quod iam praefoderat stands in front of its own antecedent aurum, which closes the sentence. All of this is Ajax's account and is itself an accusation.

sentences.t:
Ergo aut exsilio vires subduxit Achivis,
aut nece:
sentences.l: So either by exile he drew strength away from the Achaeans, or by killing:
sentences.i: So either by banishment or by murder he has drained the Achaeans of strength:
sentences.n: Vires is the plural of vis, “strength, forces”, and Achivis is a dative of separation with subduxit, “withdrew from the Achaeans”. Exsilio and nece are ablatives of means, and Ovid holds nece back to the start of line 62 so that the second answer lands on its own. Nex is a killing, not death in general.

sentences.t: sic pugnat, sic est metuendus Ulixes.
sentences.l: thus does Ulysses fight, thus is he to be feared.
sentences.n: Metuendus is a gerundive used as a predicate, “to be feared”. The two sic clauses are sarcasm: Ajax has just defined Ulysses' fighting as exile and murder, and now calls that his way of being formidable.

sentences.t:
Qui licet eloquio fidum quoque Nestora vincat,
haud tamen efficiet, desertum ut Nestora crimen
esse rear nullum.
sentences.l: Though in eloquence he may outdo even faithful Nestor, he will still not bring it about that I think the abandoning of Nestor no crime.
sentences.i: He may beat even loyal Nestor for eloquence; he will still not talk me into thinking that leaving Nestor behind was no crime.
sentences.n: Licet with the subjunctive vincat is concessive, “granted that he may outdo”. Qui opens the sentence as a connecting relative, “and he”. Quoque here is the plain adverb “even, also” — always worth checking, since the same letters can be quo-que, “and by which”. Efficiet ut ... rear is “bring it about that I think”, with ut postponed inside its own clause, standing fifth in line 64, after desertum. Within it comes the accusative and infinitive desertum Nestora ... crimen esse nullum, Nestora being a Greek accusative.

sentences.t:
Qui cum imploraret Ulixem
vulnere tardus equi fessusque senilibus annis,
proditus a socio est.
sentences.l: And he, when he was begging Ulysses for help, slowed by his horse's wound and worn out by his old man's years, was betrayed by his comrade.
sentences.i: And when Nestor was calling on Ulysses for help — held up by a wound to his horse, and tired out by his years — he was betrayed by his own ally.
sentences.n: Qui is again a connecting relative, “and he”, picking up Nestor. Cum imploraret is circumstantial cum with the imperfect subjunctive, “when he was imploring”. Vulnere ... equi is an ablative of cause with tardus, “by the wound of his horse”: it is the horse that is wounded, not Nestor. Socius is the word for an ally or comrade in arms, and Ajax puts it where it hurts most — betrayed by the man whose very title was comrade.

sentences.t:
Non haec mihi crimina fingi
scit bene Tydides, qui nomine saepe vocatum
corripuit trepidoque fugam exprobravit amico.
sentences.l: That these charges are not invented by me, Tydeus' son knows well, who often upbraided him, called by name, and reproached his panicking friend with his flight.
sentences.i: That I am not making these charges up, Diomedes knows perfectly well — he called out to him by name again and again and rebuked him, and threw his flight in the face of his frightened friend.
sentences.n: Fingi is a passive infinitive in indirect statement after scit, and mihi is a dative of agent, “by me”, which Latin allows with passive forms. Tydides is the patronymic of Diomedes, who is named outright at lines 100 and 102. Nomine ... vocatum is a participle agreeing with the unexpressed object of corripuit. Exprobrare takes the accusative of the thing thrown up, fugam, and the dative of the person, amico; calling him amico there is Ajax's sarcasm.

sentences.t: Adspiciunt oculis superi mortalia iustis!
sentences.l: The gods above look on mortal affairs with just eyes!
sentences.n: Superi, “those above”, is the subject, mortalia, “mortal things”, the object. Oculis ... iustis is an ablative of manner pulled apart so that the phrase encloses superi mortalia, the gods and the human business they are watching. The exclamation is grimly triumphant, not pious: what follows at once is offered as the proof, and as the gods' own verdict.

sentences.t:
En eget auxilio, qui non tulit, utque reliquit,
sic linquendus erat: legem sibi dixerat ipse.
sentences.l: See, he needs help, the man who brought none, and as he abandoned, so he ought to have been abandoned: he had laid down the rule for himself.
sentences.i: Look: he needs help now, the man who gave none — and as he left others, so he deserved to be left. He had set the terms himself.
sentences.n: Egeo takes the ablative auxilio. Tulit is fero in the sense “bring, render”, with auxilium understood from the words before. Linquendus erat is a gerundive with the imperfect of esse, “he was one who ought to be abandoned”; note the shift from relinquo to the simple linquo. Legem sibi dicere is a legal idiom, “to lay down a rule for oneself”, and the argument is that Ulysses' own conduct set the precedent that now binds him.

sentences.t:
Conclamat socios: adsum videoque trementem
pallentemque metu et metuentem morte futura;
sentences.l: He shouts for his comrades: I am there, and I see him trembling and pale with fear and afraid at the death to come;
sentences.i: He yells for his comrades. I am there — and I see him shaking, white with fear, terrified of the death coming for him;
sentences.n: Conclamat, adsum and video are presents set among the perfects around them, the historic present bringing the rescue up close. Metu is an ablative of cause with pallentem. Morte futura with metuentem is harder: metuo normally takes an accusative object, so the ablative is best read as cause, “afraid because of the death to come”. Magnus prints metuentem; some editions print trepidantem, “quaking at”, which the ablative suits more easily.

sentences.t:
opposui molem clipei texique iacentem
servavique animam (minimum est hic laudis) inertem.
sentences.l: I put the mass of my shield in the way and covered him as he lay, and saved his spiritless life — there is very little glory in this.
sentences.i: I threw the bulk of my shield across him and covered him where he lay, and saved his coward's life — small credit in that.
sentences.n: Opposui, texi and servavi are perfects, the deed itself after the present-tense approach to it. Iacentem, “him lying there”, is the object of texi with no pronoun expressed. Minimum ... laudis is a partitive genitive, “the least of praise”, and hic is the adverb “in this”; some editions print hoc, an ablative, “by this”. Inertem is Ajax's word for the life he saved — iners is inactive, useless, gutless — and the parenthesis is sarcasm aimed as much at the deed as at the man.

sentences.t:
Si perstas certare, locum redeamus in illum:
redde hostem vulnusque tuum solitumque timorem
post clipeumque late et mecum contende sub illo!
sentences.l: If you persist in contending, let us go back to that place: give back the enemy and your wound and your usual fear, and lie hidden behind my shield, and contend with me under it!
sentences.i: If you insist on this contest, let us go back to that spot: bring back the enemy, and your wound, and your habitual terror, and get behind my shield and fight it out with me under there!
sentences.n: Late is the imperative of lateo “lie hid”, not the adverb late “widely”: post clipeum is “behind the shield”, and the -que attached to clipeum joins the clauses. Redeamus is hortatory. Redde, “give back”, treats the enemy and the wound as things Ulysses would have to produce again for a fair re-run. Contende is the verb Ajax used at line 9 of contending in words; here he offers to settle the case by the other kind of contest.

sentences.t:
At postquam eripui, cui standi vulnera vires
non dederant, nullo tardatus vulnere fugit.
sentences.l: But after I snatched him away, the man to whom his wounds had given no strength for standing, slowed by no wound at all, fled.
sentences.i: But once I had got him out, the man whose wounds had left him no strength to stand on ran for it — and no wound slowed him down.
sentences.n: Standi is a genitive gerund depending on vires, “strength of standing”. The relative clause cui ... non dederant is itself the subject of fugit, with no pronoun expressed. The sarcasm turns on the repetition of vulnera and vulnere: the wounds that would not let him stand were no hindrance to running.

sentences.t:
Hector adest secumque deos in proelia ducit,
quaque ruit, non tu tantum terreris, Ulixe,
sed fortes etiam: tantum trahit ille timoris.
sentences.l: Hector is at hand and brings the gods with him into battle, and wherever he charges, not only you are terrified, Ulysses, but the brave too: so much fear does he drag along with him.
sentences.i: Hector comes on, bringing the gods with him into the fighting, and wherever he charges it is not only you who panic, Ulysses — even brave men do. That is how much terror he trails behind him.
sentences.n: Qua is the adverb “where, by what route”, with -que attached, “and wherever”. Tantum occurs twice in different senses: first the adverb “only”, then a noun-like “so much” governing the partitive genitive timoris. Terreris is second person passive and Ulixe is the vocative of the name — Ajax has turned from the assembly to the man himself, as he turned to the son of Poeas at line 45.

sentences.t:
Hunc ego sanguineae successu caedis ovantem
eminus ingenti resupinum pondere fudi,
hunc ego poscentem, cum quo concurreret, unus
sustinui, sortemque meam vovistis, Achivi,
et vestrae valuere preces!
sentences.l: Him, exulting at the success of a bloody slaughter, I laid low from a distance on his back with a huge weight; him, when he was demanding someone to close with, I alone withstood, and you prayed for my lot, Achaeans, and your prayers prevailed!
sentences.i: It was him — triumphant in the middle of a bloody killing — that I brought down flat on his back from a distance with one huge mass; him, when he called for someone to meet him, that I faced alone; and you prayed for my lot to come out, Achaeans, and your prayers were answered!
sentences.n: Hunc ego ... hunc ego is anaphora, two halves of one claim. Resupinum is proleptic: he was not on his back until the throw put him there, so the adjective states the result. Eminus is “from a distance”, the opposite of hand-to-hand. Cum quo concurreret is a subjunctive relative clause after poscentem, “someone with whom he might engage”. Sortem meam vovistis points to a drawing of lots, voveo being “vow for, pray for”. Valuere is the poetic third-plural perfect again, matching consedere in line 1.

sentences.t:
Si quaeritis huius
fortunam pugnae, non sum superatus ab illo.
sentences.l: If you ask the outcome of this fight, I was not beaten by him.
sentences.i: If you want to know how that fight came out: he did not beat me.
sentences.n: Quaeritis is quaero in its courtroom sense, “to inquire into” a matter. Huius ... pugnae is split across the line-end, huius closing line 89 and fortunam pugnae opening line 90. Non sum superatus is deliberate understatement: Ajax claims only that he was not beaten, which is as far as the facts he is citing will carry him.

sentences.t:
Ecce ferunt Troes ferrumque ignesque Iovemque
in Danaas classes: ubi nunc facundus Ulixes?
sentences.l: Look, the Trojans are bringing iron and fires and Jupiter against the Danaan fleet: where now is eloquent Ulysses?
sentences.i: Look — the Trojans are carrying steel and fire and Jupiter himself down on the Greek fleet: where is the eloquent Ulysses now?
sentences.n: Ferrum is “iron” for the weapons made of it. Putting Iovem third in the list treats the god as one more thing the Trojans bring to the attack, his favour or his lightning. The tripled -que ... -que ... -que is a verse mannerism for a fast list. Facundus is sarcasm here; at line 127 the narrator uses the same adjective, there of Ulysses' words, and means it.

sentences.t:
Nempe ego mille meo protexi pectore puppes,
spem vestri reditus: date pro tot navibus arma!
sentences.l: It was I, surely, who covered a thousand sterns with my own breast, the hope of your return: give arms in return for so many ships!
sentences.i: It was I, was it not, who shielded a thousand ships with my own body — your one hope of getting home: give me the arms in return for that fleet!
sentences.n: Nempe, “surely, of course”, presses a point the hearers are not expected to deny. Puppes, “sterns”, stands for whole ships, and spem vestri reditus is in apposition to it: the ships are the hope of return. Vestri is the genitive of vos going with reditus. Pro here is the preposition “in return for”, not the interjection of line 5.

sentences.t:
Quod si vera licet mihi dicere, quaeritur istis,
quam mihi, maior honos, coniunctaque gloria nostra est,
atque Aiax armis, non Aiaci arma petuntur.
sentences.l: But if I am allowed to speak the truth, a greater honour is being sought for those arms than for me, and our glory has been joined together, and Ajax is sought for the arms, not the arms for Ajax.
sentences.i: And if I may say what is true, those arms stand to gain more honour than I do; our glory is bound together now, and it is Ajax the arms need, not the arms Ajax.
sentences.n: Quod si is “but if”, the quod loosely connecting to what went before. Quaeritur is a passive with two datives of interest, istis for the arms and mihi for the speaker, and maior honos as its subject. The closing line turns on case-endings alone: Aiax nominative with armis dative, then Aiaci dative with arma nominative, the same two words trading places and functions. Ajax names himself in the third person again, as at line 17.

sentences.t:
Conferat his Ithacus Rhesum imbellemque Dolona
Priamidenque Helenum rapta cum Pallade captum:
sentences.l: Let the Ithacan set against these Rhesus, and unwarlike Dolon, and Priam's son Helenus taken along with the stolen Pallas:
sentences.i: Let the man from Ithaca line up against them his Rhesus, and Dolon, who was no fighter, and Helenus son of Priam captured along with the stolen image of Pallas:
sentences.n: Conferat is jussive, and confero takes the dative his, “compare with these”. Ithacus, “the Ithacan”, is one of the by-names Ajax uses instead of the man's own; Dulichius at line 107 is another. Priamiden keeps its Greek accusative. Pallas here is the goddess's image, the Palladium, with rapta agreeing with it in the phrase with cum, while captum agrees with Helenum. Imbellem, “unwarlike”, is Ajax's dismissal of Dolon and of the whole night's work.

sentences.t: luce nihil gestum est, nihil est Diomede remoto.
sentences.l: nothing was done in daylight, nothing with Diomedes taken away.
sentences.i: not one of them done by daylight, not one of them done once you take Diomedes out of it.
sentences.n: Luce is an ablative of time, “by day”. Diomede remoto is an ablative absolute, the same construction as vulgi stante corona in line 1: subtract Diomedes and nothing on the list stands. Magnus prints est twice, once in each half; the participle gestum has to be understood again in the second, where only est stands. The two witnesses differ over one of the two, which does not change the sense, since Latin drops the copula freely.

sentences.t:
Si semel ista datis meritis tam vilibus arma,
dividite, et pars sit maior Diomedis in illis!
sentences.l: If you once give those arms for merits so cheap, divide them, and let Diomedes' share in them be the greater!
sentences.i: If you are really going to hand over those arms for services as cheap as that, split them — and let Diomedes have the bigger share!
sentences.n: Si semel, “if once”, concedes the case for the sake of argument. Meritis is a dative with datis, “give for merits”, and vilibus is Ajax's valuation of them: vilis is the word for goods that are cheap in the market. Sit is jussive. Ista arma is the second-person demonstrative, the arms as the assembly has them in hand to give away — not the contemptuous iste Ajax reserves for Ulysses at lines 19, 37, 58 and 117.

sentences.t:
Quo tamen haec Ithaco, qui clam, qui semper inermis
rem gerit et furtis incautum decipit hostem?
sentences.l: Yet to what end are these things for the Ithacan, who in secret, who always unarmed, does his business, and cheats an unwary enemy by thefts?
sentences.i: And what would the Ithacan want them for anyway — a man who does his work under cover, who is never armed, who tricks an enemy off his guard by thieving?
sentences.n: Quo is “to what end, for what purpose”, and there is no verb: sunt has to be supplied with haec. Rem gerere is the standard phrase for conducting an operation, military or public, so Ajax grants that Ulysses does the business while denying that it is soldiering. The first qui clause has no verb of its own and leans on the gerit of the second: qui clam, qui semper inermis rem gerit. Furtis, “by thefts”, repeats the accusation of line 32 and is picked up again by ad furta at line 111.

sentences.t:
Ipse nitor galeae claro radiantis ab auro
insidias prodet manifestabitque latentem.
sentences.l: The very gleam of the helmet, radiant with bright gold, will betray his ambushes and will show him up as he lurks.
sentences.i: The shine of that helmet, blazing with bright gold, will give his ambushes away and expose him in hiding.
sentences.n: Ipse nitor, “the gleam itself”, makes the helmet the informer. Prodet is the verb used at line 59 of betraying the Danaan cause and at line 67 of Nestor being betrayed, so the helmet does to Ulysses what Ajax says he does to others. Claro ... ab auro is the source of the radiance, ab with the ablative, and radiantis stands between the adjective and its noun. Latentem is a participle used as the object, “the man hiding”.

sentences.t:
Sed neque Dulichius sub Achillis casside vertex
pondera tanta feret, nec non onerosa gravisque
Pelias hasta potest imbellibus esse lacertis,
nec clipeus vasti concretus imagine mundi
conveniet timidae nataeque ad furta sinistrae:
sentences.l: But neither will the Dulichian head under Achilles' helmet bear such weights, nor can the Pelian spear fail to be burdensome and heavy to unwarlike arms, nor will the shield formed with the image of the vast world suit a left hand that is timid and born for thefts:
sentences.i: But that Dulichian head will not carry such a weight under Achilles' helmet; the spear from Pelion cannot be anything but a burden and a drag on unwarlike arms; and the shield with the whole vast world worked into it will never suit a left hand that is timid and made for stealing:
sentences.n: Three limbs on neque ... nec ... nec. The middle one carries a double negative: nec ... non onerosa gravisque potest esse is “cannot fail to be burdensome and heavy”, so the litotes asserts the opposite of what the words look like at first glance. Dulichius and Pelias are both place-adjectives, the one from an island of Ulysses' realm, the other from Mount Pelion, where the wood of the spear came from. Concretus is “compacted, formed”; some editions print caelatus, “chased, embossed”, which makes the world a worked relief rather than the stuff the shield is made of. Sinistrae is a dative, the shield hand, and natae ad furta, “born for thefts”, is the charge once more.

sentences.t: debilitaturum quid te petis, Improbe, munus?
sentences.l: Why do you seek a gift that will cripple you, shameless creature?
sentences.n: Debilitaturum is a future active participle agreeing with munus and governing te, “a gift about to weaken you” — Latin uses the future participle where English needs a relative clause. Improbe is a vocative set between the verb petis and its object munus: improbus is “shameless, without restraint”, and it is one of the hardest words Ajax throws. Munus is the armour considered as a gift in the assembly's keeping. Magnus prints Improbe with a capital I in mid-line; it is an ordinary vocative adjective here and not a name, and the text is given exactly as the edition prints it.

sentences.t:
Quod tibi si populi donaverit error Achivi,
cur spolieris, erit, non cur metuaris ab hoste,
et fuga, qua sola cunctos, timidissime, vincis,
tarda futura tibi est gestamina tanta trahenti.
sentences.l: But if the Achaean people's error shall have granted this to you, there will be reason why you should be stripped of it, not why you should be feared by the enemy, and flight, the one thing in which you beat everybody, you utter coward, will be slow for you as you drag such great gear.
sentences.i: And if the Achaean people's blunder does hand it to you, you will have given the enemy a reason to strip you, not a reason to fear you; and running away, the one event you win, you supreme coward, will be slow work with all that equipment to drag.
sentences.n: Quod is a connecting relative and the object of donaverit, “and if the error shall have given this to you”; donaverit is future perfect. Erit governs two cur clauses whose verbs, spolieris and metuaris, are subjunctives, “there will be a reason why you should be stripped”. Populi ... Achivi is a genitive pair with donaverit error standing inside it. Timidissime is a vocative superlative and the contempt is unmistakable: the one contest Ulysses wins is running. Trahenti agrees with tibi.

sentences.t:
Adde quod iste tuus, tam raro proelia passus,
integer est clipeus:
sentences.l: Add that that shield of yours, having suffered battles so rarely, is undamaged:
sentences.i: And another thing: that shield of yours has been in so few fights that it is still whole:
sentences.n: Adde quod is the idiom “add the fact that”. Passus is the participle of the deponent patior, passive in form and active in meaning, “having undergone”. Integer is “untouched, unhurt”. Iste tuus keeps the contemptuous demonstrative, and its noun clipeus is held back to line 118.

sentences.t:
nostro, qui tela ferendo
mille patet plagis, novus est successor habendus.
sentences.l: for mine, which gapes with a thousand gashes from carrying weapons, a new successor must be got.
sentences.i: mine, split open by a thousand blows from taking weapons, needs a replacement.
sentences.n: Nostro is a dative of the thing concerned, with clipeo understood from the line before. Tela ferendo is a gerund with an accusative object, the same licence as volucres petendo at line 53. Patet is “stands open”, with plagis the ablative of the gashes that open it. Habendus est is a gerundive of obligation, “must be got”. Successor is the word used at line 51 of the man who inherited Hercules' arrows: the shield too needs an heir.

sentences.t: Denique (quid verbis opus est?) spectemur agendo!
sentences.l: In short — what need is there of words? — let us be looked at in the doing!
sentences.i: Enough of words — let us be watched in action!
sentences.n: Opus est takes the ablative verbis, “there is need of words”. Spectemur is a jussive passive, “let us be looked at, put on view”. Agendo is an ablative gerund of ago, the verb of causam agimus at lines 5 and 6, where Ajax began by pleading a case: he ends by asking that the case be settled by doing instead, and the play on the one verb is the point of the line.

sentences.t:
Arma viri fortis medios mittantur in hostes:
inde iubete peti et referentem ornate relatis?”
sentences.l: Let the arms of the brave man be thrown into the midst of the enemy: order them to be fetched from there, and adorn the man who brings them back with what he has brought back!
sentences.i: Throw the brave man's arms into the thick of the enemy: give the order to go and get them, and decorate whoever brings them back with what he brings!
sentences.n: Mittantur is a jussive passive; iubete and ornate are plain imperatives, and iubete peti is “order them to be sought”, with a passive infinitive and no subject expressed. Referentem ... relatis sets the present participle of refero beside the ablative of its own perfect participle, the same verb doing two jobs, which English has to unpack. The edition closes the speech with a question mark after relatis although the sentence is a string of commands with nothing interrogative in it; the sense wants a full stop or an exclamation mark. The text is given here exactly as Magnus prints it, unaltered.

sentences.t:
Finierat Telamone satus vulgique secutum
ultima murmur erat, donec Laertius heros
adstitit atque oculos paulum tellure moratos
sustulit ad proceres exspectatoque resolvit
ora sono;
sentences.l: The son of Telamon had finished, and the murmur of the crowd had followed his last words, until the Laertian hero stood forward and lifted his eyes, lingering a little on the ground, to the chiefs, and unsealed his mouth in the sound they had been waiting for.
sentences.i: Telamon's son had finished, and a murmur from the crowd came after his closing words, until the hero of Laertes' line stood up, raised his eyes — they had rested a moment on the ground — to the chiefs, and opened his lips on the voice they had been waiting for.
sentences.n: Satus with the ablative Telamone is the third participle of origin in this part, after creatus at line 22 and cretus at line 31. Secutum erat is a pluperfect of the deponent sequor, active in meaning, with ultima, “his last words”, as its object. Moratos is likewise a deponent participle with active force, “having lingered”, agreeing with oculos. Exspectato ... sono is an ablative with resolvit, the sound the assembly had been waiting for. Ora is the poetic plural for the mouth.

sentences.t: neque abest facundis gratia dictis.
sentences.l: nor is charm absent from his eloquent words.
sentences.n: Abest here takes the dative dictis, “is lacking to”. The tense shifts to the present after the pluperfects before it, bringing the reader up to the moment of speaking. Facundis agrees with dictis: it is the narrator's own word for Ulysses' speech, the adjective Ajax threw at the man himself sarcastically at line 92, and here it is meant.

sentences.t:
“Si mea cum vestris valuissent vota, Pelasgi,
non foret ambiguus tanti certaminis heres,
tuque tuis armis, nos te poteremur, Achille.
sentences.l: “If my prayers had prevailed along with yours, Pelasgians, the heir of so great a contest would not be in doubt, and you would have your own arms, Achilles, and we would have you.
sentences.i: “If my prayers had counted for anything alongside yours, Pelasgians, there would be no question who inherits this great contest: you would still have your arms, Achilles, and we would still have you.
sentences.n: Valuissent is a pluperfect subjunctive of the unreal past, and it answers valuere at line 89, where Ajax said the Greeks' prayers did prevail. Foret is an old alternative to esset. The single verb poteremur, first person plural, has to serve the second-person tu as well, with the person silently adjusted — a compression verse allows. Potior governs the ablative in tuis armis and the accusative in nos te, and both constructions belong to the verb. Achille is a vocative: Ulysses turns aside to address the dead man, as Ajax turned aside at lines 45 and 83.

sentences.t:
Quem quoniam non aequa mihi vobisque negarunt
fata” (manuque simul veluti lacrimantia tersit
lumina), “quis magno melius succedit Achilli,
quam per quem magnus Danais successit Achilles?
sentences.l: And since fates not fair to me and to you have denied him us” — and at the same time he wiped with his hand eyes that seemed to be weeping — “who succeeds great Achilles better than the man through whom great Achilles came to the Danaans?
sentences.i: “And since fates unfair to me and to you have taken him from us” — and as he said it he drew his hand across eyes that looked as if they were weeping — “who is a better successor to great Achilles than the man through whom great Achilles came to the Greeks?
sentences.n: Quem is a connecting relative, “and him”, the object of negarunt, which is the syncopated perfect for negaverunt. Non aequa ... fata is “fates not fair”, with mihi and vobis datives after aequa. The parenthesis is the poem speaking, not Ulysses, and veluti, “as if”, is the poem's word: it leaves the tears unauthenticated. Succedit takes the dative Achilli, and the name returns as the nominative Achilles at the end of the next line, each time with a form of magnus beside it — magno Achilli, then magnus ... Achilles. Magnus prints the indicative succedit; some editions print the subjunctive succedat, which would make the question a deliberative one, “who is to succeed?”.

sentences.t:
Huic modo ne prosit, quod, uti est, hebes esse videtur,
neve mihi noceat, quod vobis semper, Achivi,
profuit ingenium, meaque haec facundia, siqua est,
quae nunc pro domino, pro vobis saepe locuta est,
invidia careat, bona nec sua quisque recuset.
sentences.l: Only let it not help him that he seems, as indeed he is, to be dull, and let it not harm me that my wit has always been of use to you, Achaeans; and let this eloquence of mine, if I have any, which now speaks for its master and has often spoken for you, be free of ill-will, and let no one refuse what is his own.
sentences.i: Only let him gain no advantage from seeming dull — as he is; and let it not count against me that my wits have always served you, Achaeans. And let this eloquence of mine, if I have any, which speaks now for its owner and has often spoken for you, escape being resented, and let nobody turn down what belongs to him.
sentences.n: Four jussive subjunctives carry the sentence: ne prosit, neve noceat, careat, recuset, with modo meaning “only”. The two quod clauses are noun clauses, each the subject of its verb: “that he seems dull”, “that my wit has been of use”. Uti is the older form of ut, “as”, and uti est is the aside — dull, and really so. Siqua is si with the indefinite qua, “if any”. Locuta est is a deponent perfect, active in sense, and one verb serves both pro domino and pro vobis saepe. Careo takes the ablative invidia. In the last clause nec is displaced to second place, after bona.
